{ mkdtemp, readFile, rm, stat } from 'fs/promises';\nimport { tmpdir } from 'os';\nimport { join } from 'path';\nimport { spaceTrim } from 'spacetrim';\nimport { $runGoScript } from './$runGoScript';\nimport { $runGoScriptUntilMarkerIdle } from './$runGoScriptUntilMarkerIdle';\nimport { $runGoScriptWithOutput } from './$runGoScriptWithOutput';\nimport { buildScriptLogPath } from './buildScriptLogPath';\n\ndescribe('runGoScript runtime logging', () => {\n    let temporaryDirectoryPath: string;\n\n    beforeEach(async () => {\n        temporaryDirectoryPath = await mkdtemp(join(tmpdir(), 'promptbook-coder-runtime-log-'));\n    });\n\n    afterEach(async () => {\n        await rm(temporaryDirectoryPath, { recursive: true, force: true });\n    });\n\n    it('logs raw input and live output into the runtime log file', async () => {\n        const scriptPath = join(temporaryDirectoryPath, 'prompt-1.sh');\n        const logPath = buildScriptLogPath(scriptPath);\n\n        const output = await $runGoScriptWithOutput({\n            scriptPath,\n            logPath,\n            scriptContent: spaceTrim(`\n                printf 'runner stdout\\\\n'\n                printf 'runner stderr\\\\n' >&2\n            `),\n        });\n\n        const log = await readFile(logPath, 'utf-8');\n\n        expect(output).toContain('runner stdout');\n        expect(output).toContain('runner stderr');\n        expect(log).toContain('=== runner shell started at ');\n        expect(log).toContain('--- raw input ---');\n        expect(log).toContain(\"printf 'runner stdout\\\\n'\");\n        expect(log).toContain('runner stdout');\n        expect(log).toContain('runner stderr');\n        expect(log).toContain('Status: succeeded');\n        await expect(stat(scriptPath)).rejects.toMatchObject({ code: 'ENOENT' });\n    });\n\n    it('keeps the temp shell file after success when preservation is enabled', async () => {\n        const scriptPath = join(temporaryDirectoryPath, 'prompt-keep.sh');\n        const logPath = buildScriptLogPath(scriptPath);\n\n        const output = await $runGoScriptWithOutput({\n            scriptPath,\n            logPath,\n            preserveArtifactsOnSuccess: true,\n            scriptContent: \"printf 'runner stdout\\\\n'\",\n        });\n\n        expect(output).toContain('runner stdout');\n        await expect(readFile(scriptPath, 'utf-8')).resolves.toContain(\"printf 'runner stdout\\\\n'\");\n    });\n\n    it('keeps both the runtime log and temp shell file after failures', async () => {\n        const scriptPath = join(temporaryDirectoryPath, 'prompt-1.test.sh');\n        const logPath = buildScriptLogPath(scriptPath);\n\n        await expect(\n            $runGoScript({\n                scriptPath,\n                logPath,\n                scriptContent: spaceTrim(`\n                    printf 'test failure\\\\n' >&2\n                    exit 2\n                `),\n            }),\n        ).rejects.toThrow();\n\n        const log = await readFile(logPath, 'utf-8');\n\n        expect(log).toContain('=== test shell started at ');\n        expect(log).toContain('test failure');\n        expect(log).toContain('Status: failed');\n        await expect(readFile(scriptPath, 'utf-8')).resolves.toContain(\"printf 'test failure\\\\n' >&2\");\n    });\n\n    it('can suppress live stdout and stderr while still capturing output and runtime logs', async () => {\n        const scriptPath = join(temporaryDirectoryPath, 'prompt-quiet.sh');\n        const logPath = buildScriptLogPath(scriptPath);\n        const consoleInfoSpy = jest.spyOn(console, 'info').mockImplementation(() => undefined);\n        const consoleWarnSpy = jest.spyOn(console, 'warn').mockImplementation(() => undefined);\n\n        try {\n            const output = await $runGoScriptUntilMarkerIdle({\n                scriptPath,\n                logPath,\n                shouldPrintLiveOutput: false,\n                completionLineMatcher: /^tokens used$/u,\n                idleTimeoutMs: 50,\n                scriptContent: spaceTrim(`\n                    printf 'runner stdout\\\\n'\n                    printf 'runner stderr\\\\n' >&2\n                    printf 'tokens used\\\\n'\n                `),\n            });\n\n            const log = await readFile(logPath, 'utf-8');\n\n            expect(output).toContain('runner stdout');\n            expect(output).toContain('runner stderr');\n            expect(log).toContain('runner stdout');\n            expect(log).toContain('runner stderr');\n            expect(consoleInfoSpy).not.toHaveBeenCalled();\n            expect(consoleWarnSpy).not.toHaveBeenCalled();\n        } finally {\n            consoleInfoSpy.mockRestore();\n            consoleWarnSpy.mockRestore();\n        }\n    });\n});\n","numLines":119,"startLine":1,"totalLines":119}}}

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01SxsrZU3ZK78CXTMjhkcZGJ","type":"tool_result","content":"40\t1. **Verified by your tests** — \"Run any test command after each prompt. When it fails, ptbk coder hands the output back to the agent, which retries until the tests pass.\"\n41\t2. **Test before coding** — \"Run the tests before the first coding prompt. Stop on failures that were already there, or let one repair prompt fix them before the backlog starts.\"\n42\t3. **Commits with its own identity** — \"Every successful round lands under a git identity that belongs to the agent, GPG-signed if you set that up. You can always tell which commits it wrote.\"\n43\t4. **Autopilot git** — \"Pull before prompts and push after commits, so a long-running queue stays in sync with your remote.\"\n44\t5. **Git-synced housekeeping** — \"ptbk coder init, add, generate-boilerplates and verify all take the same --commit, --auto-push and --auto-pull switches. Setting up a project, queueing prompts and archiving finished ones leave no uncommitted work behind. Verify pulls and pushes around every single verification.\"\n45\t6. **Isolated worktrees** — \"Implement every prompt in its own temporary git worktree with its own environment. Verified work lands back on your branch as one commit. If a task will not merge, ptbk coder marks it failed and keeps its worktree so you can look at it. Deeply nested repositories work on Windows too.\"\n46\t7. **Kanban web UI** — \"ptbk coder server keeps running after the queue is empty, watches for new prompt files and serves a Trello-style board where you can edit prompts in the browser.\"\n47\t8. **Prompt priorities** — \"Give prompts a priority and process only the range you want in the current run.\"\n48\t9. **Model-specific prompts** — \"Route a prompt to a model family or harness with a backtick token on its [ ] status line, such as [ ] use model `gpt-5.5`. Other runners skip it.\"\n49\t10. **Agent-specific prompts** — \"Route a prompt to the selected Book with its path, filename, stem or title from the first line, such as [ ] use agent `developer`. Other agents skip it.\"\n50\t11. **Pacing and retries** — \"Wait a fixed wall-clock duration between prompts. The clock keeps running through a pause and through sleep, and errors retry after a cool-down. The terminal also shows every subscription window a harness reports, with its remaining allowance and reset time. Whenever S is offered it skips whatever the coder waits for right now, down to the harness session limit that would otherwise hold the run for hours.\"\n51\t12. **List before you run** — \"See every ready, fully authored prompt grouped by priority before starting a harness. Narrow the list by harness, model, agent, or priority range; no files change and no tokens are spent.\"\n52\t13. **Ping before you queue** — \"ptbk coder ping sends one tiny dummy prompt to a harness and model and reports the answer, the response time and the usage. Use it to check that a harness, model and login work before you queue anything. It also opens the hourly or weekly quota window early, so the quota is already refreshing by the time you need it. If that harness has missing local ignore rules, it asks before adding them to .gitignore.\"\n53\t14. **Keep the 5-hour window rolling** — \"Add --period and the ping repeats until you stop it with CTRL+C. One ping every 5h holds the Claude Code 5-hour limit window open, so a queue you start at any hour already has a refreshing window waiting for it. That costs a handful of tokens per ping instead of a run you have to babysit.\"\n54\t15. **Human in the loop** — \"Confirm each prompt yourself with --no-auto. Press P to pause a running queue, or X to end it after the current prompt. Every press is answered in the Controls panel on the next frame, so you can tell that the key landed even when it changed nothing.\"\n55\t16. **Nothing to answer** — \"The opposite end: --no-questions never asks anything at all. Installing a missing harness, updating an outdated one or adding ignore rules is skipped and printed as the command which does it manually, so a queue started from a script or a CI job never stops at a prompt nobody is there to answer. ptbk coder init, add, run, ping and server all take it.\"\n56\t17. **Live status in the prompt file** — \"A [ ] prompt — or plain markdown with no status checkbox — turns into [^] the moment the agent picks it up, and the line names the step that is running. A run started with --agent names that agent in front of its harness, so a finished prompt says which agent implemented it. A prompt without a checkbox starts at priority 0. Use [-] or [.] to keep a task out of the queue, or add `<!--ptbk-coder-ignore-->` anywhere in a Markdown file to ignore it entirely. It only becomes [x] after the work is implemented, verified and committed. ptbk coder never reverts a [^], so if the queue is killed or crashes you can see which task was left half-done.\"\n57\t18. **Pick up where the run stopped** — \"A dirty working tree stops ptbk coder by default. --git-changes ignore starts anyway, and --git-changes continue resumes the one prompt left in [^] with its half-finished changes still in place. Any harness can take the work over, and the status line then names both the one that started and the one that finished it.\"\n58\t19. **Run traces you can read later** — \"Every round leaves a trace in prompts/traces/, named after the prompt file it belongs to. It holds the agent, harness, model, thinking level and login method that ran the prompt, what each step cost and how long it took, and the whole raw output of the harness. The trace is committed together with the prompt, so the run can still be analyzed long after its temporary logs are gone.\"\n59\t20. **Verify and archive** — \"Every successful round writes the agent, harness, model and thinking level into the prompt status line. Walk through completed prompts one by one, archive the finished ones to prompts/done/, and get a repair prompt appended for anything left incomplete. Pick the order with --order from-earliest, from-latest or random.\""}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"74608ceb-c452-4e82-b385-4ad6b325ff5b","uuid":"42e2c996-d668-41e6-bfe3-68ad69c4ba2b","timestamp":"2026-09-17T16:27:51.237Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\\Users\\me\\work\\ai\\promptbook\\apps\\coder-landing\\specs\\sections\\advanced-features.md","content":"1. **Verified by your tests** — \"Run any test command after each prompt. Whenever S is offered it skips whatever the coder waits for right now, down to the harness session limit that would otherwise hold the run for hours.\"","originalFile":"# Section: Advanced features\n\nAnchor `#features`. A grid of feature cards, each pairing a short explanation with a terminal snippet — covering the \"everything around the agent\" machinery from [`../product.md`](../product.md).\n\n## Copy\n\n-   **Heading**: `Built for unattended coding` (\"unattended\" in Promptbook Blue).\n-   **Lead paragraph**: The agent writes the code. ptbk coder does the rest: it runs your tests, commits, pulls and pushes, paces the queue against your quota window, and gives you back control the moment you press P or X. That is what keeps a run going for hours without you.\n\n## Cards\n\n3-column grid on desktop, 2 on tablet, 1 on mobile. Each card: title (Outfit semibold), description, and a [terminal block](../components/terminal-block.md) snippet. Exactly these twenty-one cards, in this order:\n\n| #   | Title                          | Snippet                                                                                          |\n| --- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |\n| 1   | Verified by your tests         | `ptbk coder run --harness claude-code --test npm test`                                           |\n| 2   | Test before coding             | `ptbk coder run --harness claude-code --test npm test --test-before yes-and-fix`                 |\n| 3   | Commits with its own identity  | `CODING_AGENT_GIT_NAME=\"Promptbook Coding Agent\"`                                                |\n| 4   | Autopilot git                  | `ptbk coder run --harness claude-code --auto-pull --auto-push`                                   |\n| 5   | Git-synced housekeeping        | `ptbk coder init --auto-pull --commit --auto-push`                                               |\n| 6   | Isolated worktrees             | `ptbk coder run --harness claude-code --isolate`                                                 |\n| 7   | Kanban web UI                  | `ptbk coder server --port 4441 --harness claude-code`                                            |\n| 8   | Prompt priorities              | `ptbk coder run --harness claude-code --min-priority 1 --max-priority 5`                         |\n| 9   | Model-specific prompts         | `ptbk coder run --harness github-copilot --model gpt-5.5`                                        |\n| 10  | Agent-specific prompts         | `ptbk coder run --harness github-copilot --model gpt-5.5 --agent agents/developer.book`         |\n| 11  | Pacing and retries             | `ptbk coder run --harness claude-code --wait-between-prompts 30m --wait-after-error 10m`         |\n| 12  | List before you run            | `ptbk coder list`                                                                                |\n| 13  | Ping before you queue          | `ptbk coder ping --harness openai-codex --model gpt-5.6-sol --thinking-level xhigh`              |\n| 14  | Keep the 5-hour window rolling | `ptbk coder ping --harness claude-code --model claude-sonnet-5 --thinking-level low --period 5h` |\n| 15  | Human in the loop              | `ptbk coder run --harness claude-code --no-auto`                                                 |\n| 16  | Nothing to answer              | `ptbk coder run --harness claude-code --no-questions`                                            |\n| 17  | Live status in the prompt file | `` [^] by Developer on OpenAI Codex `gpt-5.6-luna` - Implementation in progress ``               |\n| 18  | Pick up where the run stopped  | `ptbk coder run --harness claude-code --git-changes continue`                                    |\n| 19  | Run traces you can read later  | `prompts/traces/2026-09-0180-add-dark-mode.md`                                                   |\n| 20  | Verify and archive             | `ptbk coder verify --order from-latest`                                                          |\n| 21  | Many prompts per file          | `ptbk coder generate-boilerplates --count 10*7`                                                  |\n\n## Descriptions (verbatim card copy)\n\n1. **Verified by your tests** — \"Run any test command after each prompt. When it fails, ptbk coder hands the output back to the agent, which retries until the tests pass.\"\n2. **Test before coding** — \"Run the tests before the first coding prompt. Stop on failures that were already there, or let one repair prompt fix them before the backlog starts.\"\n3. **Commits with its own identity** — \"Every successful round lands under a git identity that belongs to the agent, GPG-signed if you set that up. You can always tell which commits it wrote.\"\n4. **Autopilot git** — \"Pull before prompts and push after commits, so a long-running queue stays in sync with your remote.\"\n5. **Git-synced housekeeping** — \"ptbk coder init, add, generate-boilerplates and verify all take the same --commit, --auto-push and --auto-pull switches. Setting up a project, queueing prompts and archiving finished ones leave no uncommitted work behind. Verify pulls and pushes around every single verification.\"\n6. **Isolated worktrees** — \"Implement every prompt in its own temporary git worktree with its own environment. Verified work lands back on your branch as one commit. If a task will not merge, ptbk coder marks it failed and keeps its worktree so you can look at it. Deeply nested repositories work on Windows too.\"\n7. **Kanban web UI** — \"ptbk coder server keeps running after the queue is empty, watches for new prompt files and serves a Trello-style board where you can edit prompts in the browser.\"\n8. **Prompt priorities** — \"Give prompts a priority and process only the range you want in the current run.\"\n9. **Model-specific prompts** — \"Route a prompt to a model family or harness with a backtick token on its [ ] status line, such as [ ] use model `gpt-5.5`. Other runners skip it.\"\n10. **Agent-specific prompts** — \"Route a prompt to the selected Book with its path, filename, stem or title from the first line, such as [ ] use agent `developer`. Other agents skip it.\"\n11. **Pacing and retries** — \"Wait a fixed wall-clock duration between prompts. The clock keeps running through a pause and through sleep, and errors retry after a cool-down. The terminal also shows every subscription window a harness reports, with its remaining allowance and reset time. Whenever S is offered it skips whatever the coder waits for right now, down to the harness session limit that would otherwise hold the run for hours.\"\n12. **List before you run** — \"See every ready, fully authored prompt grouped by priority before starting a harness. Narrow the list by harness, model, agent, or priority range; no files change and no tokens are spent.\"\n13. **Ping before you queue** — \"ptbk coder ping sends one tiny dummy prompt to a harness and model and reports the answer, the response time and the usage. Use it to check that a harness, model and login work before you queue anything. It also opens the hourly or weekly quota window early, so the quota is already refreshing by the time you need it. If that harness has missing local ignore rules, it asks before adding them to .gitignore.\"\n14. **Keep the 5-hour window rolling** — \"Add --period and the ping repeats until you stop it with CTRL+C. One ping every 5h holds the Claude Code 5-hour limit window open, so a queue you start at any hour already has a refreshing window waiting for it. That costs a handful of tokens per ping instead of a run you have to babysit.\"\n15. **Human in the loop** — \"Confirm each prompt yourself with --no-auto. Press P to pause a running queue, or X to end it after the current prompt. Every press is answered in the Controls panel on the next frame, so you can tell that the key landed even when it changed nothing.\"\n16. **Nothing to answer** — \"The opposite end: --no-questions never asks anything at all. Installing a missing harness, updating an outdated one or adding ignore rules is skipped and printed as the command which does it manually, so a queue started from a script or a CI job never stops at a prompt nobody is there to answer. ptbk coder init, add, run, ping and server all take it.\"\n17. **Live status in the prompt file** — \"A [ ] prompt — or plain markdown with no status checkbox — turns into [^] the moment the agent picks it up, and the line names the step that is running. A run started with --agent names that agent in front of its harness, so a finished prompt says which agent implemented it. A prompt without a checkbox starts at priority 0. Use [-] or [.] to keep a task out of the queue, or add `<!--ptbk-coder-ignore-->` anywhere in a Markdown file to ignore it entirely. It only becomes [x] after the work is implemented, verified and committed. ptbk coder never reverts a [^], so if the queue is killed or crashes you can see which task was left half-done.\"\n18. **Pick up where the run stopped** — \"A dirty working tree stops ptbk coder by default. --git-changes ignore starts anyway, and --git-changes continue resumes the one prompt left in [^] with its half-finished changes still in place. Any harness can take the work over, and the status line then names both the one that started and the one that finished it.\"\n19. **Run traces you can read later** — \"Every round leaves a trace in prompts/traces/, named after the prompt file it belongs to. It holds the agent, harness, model, thinking level and login method that ran the prompt, what each step cost and how long it took, and the whole raw output of the harness. The trace is committed together with the prompt, so the run can still be analyzed long after its temporary logs are gone.\"\n20. **Verify and archive** — \"Every successful round writes the agent, harness, model and thinking level into the prompt status line. Walk through completed prompts one by one, archive the finished ones to prompts/done/, and get a repair prompt appended for anything left incomplete. Pick the order with --order from-earliest, from-latest or random.\"\n21. **Many prompts per file** — \"ptbk coder generate-boilerplates writes one prompt per file by default (--count 5\\*1). Use --count N\\*M to pack a whole backlog into fewer files: N files with M prompts each. A --- line separates the sections, every file carries one fresh emoji tag, and each section still runs as its own task.\"\n\nOption semantics must stay consistent with [`../content/commands.md`](../content/commands.md).\n","structuredPatch":[{"oldStart":47,"oldLines":7,"newStart":47,"newLines":7,"lines":[" 8. **Prompt priorities** — \"Give prompts a priority and process only the range you want in the current run.\""," 9. **Model-specific prompts** — \"Route a prompt to a model family or harness with a backtick token on its [ ] status line, such as [ ] use model `gpt-5.5`. When it fails, ptbk coder hands the output back to the agent, which retries until the tests pass.',\n        sampleCommand: 'ptbk coder run --harness claude-code --test npm test',\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'Test before coding',\n        description:\n            'Run the tests before the first coding prompt. Stop on failures that were already there, or let one repair prompt fix them before the backlog starts.',\n        sampleCommand: TEST_BEFORE_FIX_COMMAND,\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'Commits with its own identity',\n        description:\n            'Every successful round lands under a git identity that belongs to the agent, GPG-signed if you set that up. You can always tell which commits it wrote.',\n        sampleCommand: 'CODING_AGENT_GIT_NAME=\"Promptbook Coding Agent\"',\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'Autopilot git',\n        description:\n            'Pull before prompts and push after commits, so a long-running queue stays in sync with your remote.',\n        sampleCommand: 'ptbk coder run --harness claude-code --auto-pull --auto-push',\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'Git-synced housekeeping',\n        description:\n            'ptbk coder init, add, generate-boilerplates and verify all take the same --commit, --auto-push and --auto-pull switches. Setting up a project, queueing prompts and archiving finished ones leave no uncommitted work behind. Verify pulls and pushes around every single verification.',\n        sampleCommand: INIT_GIT_SYNC_COMMAND,\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'Isolated worktrees',\n        description:\n            'Implement every prompt in its own temporary git worktree with its own environment. Verified work lands back on your branch as one commit. If a task will not merge, ptbk coder marks it failed and keeps its worktree so you can look at it. Deeply nested repositories work on Windows too.',\n        sampleCommand: 'ptbk coder run --harness claude-code --isolate',\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'Kanban web UI',\n        description:\n            'ptbk coder server keeps running after the queue is empty, watches for new prompt files and serves a Trello-style board where you can edit prompts in the browser.',\n        sampleCommand: 'ptbk coder server --port 4441 --harness claude-code',\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'Prompt priorities',\n        description: 'Give prompts a priority and process only the range you want in the current run.',\n        sampleCommand: 'ptbk coder run --harness claude-code --min-priority 1 --max-priority 5',\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'Model-specific prompts',\n        description:\n            'Route a prompt to a model family or harness with a backtick token on its [ ] status line, such as [ ] use model `gpt-5.5`. Other runners skip it.',\n        sampleCommand: MODEL_FILTER_COMMAND,\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'Agent-specific prompts',\n        description:\n            'Route a prompt to the selected Book with its path, filename, stem or title from the first line, such as [ ] use agent `developer`. Other agents skip it.',\n        sampleCommand: AGENT_FILTER_COMMAND,\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'Pacing and retries',\n        description:\n            'Wait a fixed wall-clock duration between prompts. The clock keeps running through a pause and through sleep, and errors retry after a cool-down. The terminal also shows every subscription window a harness reports, with its remaining allowance and reset time. Whenever S is offered it skips whatever the coder waits for right now, down to the harness session limit that would otherwise hold the run for hours.',\n        sampleCommand: 'ptbk coder run --harness claude-code --wait-between-prompts 30m --wait-after-error 10m',\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'List before you run',\n        description:\n            'See every ready, fully authored prompt grouped by priority before starting a harness. Narrow the list by harness, model, agent, or priority range; no files change and no tokens are spent.',\n        sampleCommand: LIST_COMMAND,\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'Ping before you queue',\n        description:\n            'ptbk coder ping sends one tiny dummy prompt to a harness and model and reports the answer, the response time and the usage. Use it to check that a harness, model and login work before you queue anything. It also opens the hourly or weekly quota window early, so the quota is already refreshing by the time you need it. If that harness has missing local ignore rules, it asks before adding them to .gitignore.',\n        sampleCommand: PING_COMMAND,\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'Keep the 5-hour window rolling',\n        description:\n            'Add --period and the ping repeats until you stop it with CTRL+C. One ping every 5h holds the Claude Code 5-hour limit window open, so a queue you start at any hour already has a refreshing window waiting for it. That costs a handful of tokens per ping instead of a run you have to babysit.',\n        sampleCommand: PING_PERIOD_COMMAND,\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'Human in the loop',\n        description:\n            'Confirm each prompt yourself with --no-auto. Press P to pause a running queue, or X to end it after the current prompt. Every press is answered in the Controls panel on the next frame, so you can tell that the key landed even when it changed nothing.',\n        sampleCommand: 'ptbk coder run --harness claude-code --no-auto',\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'Nothing to answer',\n        description:\n            'The opposite end: --no-questions never asks anything at all. Installing a missing harness, updating an outdated one or adding ignore rules is skipped and printed as the command which does it manually, so a queue started from a script or a CI job never stops at a prompt nobody is there to answer. ptbk coder init, add, run, ping and server all take it.',\n        sampleCommand: 'ptbk coder run --harness claude-code --no-questions',\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'Live status in the prompt file',\n        description:\n            'A [ ] prompt — or plain markdown with no status checkbox — turns into [^] the moment the agent picks it up, and the line names the step that is running. A run started with --agent names that agent in front of its harness, so a finished prompt says which agent implemented it. A prompt without a checkbox starts at priority 0. Use [-] or [.] to keep a task out of the queue, or add <!--ptbk-coder-ignore--> anywhere in a Markdown file to ignore it entirely. It only becomes [x] after the work is implemented, verified and committed. ptbk coder never reverts a [^], so if the queue is killed or crashes you can see which task was left half-done.',\n        sampleCommand: '[^] by Developer on OpenAI Codex `gpt-5.6-luna` - Implementation in progress',\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'Pick up where the run stopped',\n        description:\n            'A dirty working tree stops ptbk coder by default. --git-changes ignore starts anyway, and --git-changes continue resumes the one prompt left in [^] with its half-finished changes still in place. Any harness can take the work over, and the status line then names both the one that started and the one that finished it.',\n        sampleCommand: GIT_CHANGES_CONTINUE_COMMAND,\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'Run traces you can read later',\n        description:\n            'Every round leaves a trace in prompts/traces/, named after the prompt file it belongs to. It holds the agent, harness, model, thinking level and login method that ran the prompt, what each step cost and how long it took, and the whole raw output of the harness. The trace is committed together with the prompt, so the run can still be analyzed long after its temporary logs are gone.',\n        sampleCommand: 'prompts/traces/2026-09-0180-add-dark-mode.md',\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'Verify and archive',\n        description:\n            'Every successful round writes the agent, harness, model and thinking level into the prompt status line. Walk through completed prompts one by one, archive the finished ones to prompts/done/, and get a repair prompt appended for anything left incomplete. Pick the order with --order from-earliest, from-latest or random.',\n        sampleCommand: VERIFY_COMMAND,\n    },\n    {\n        title: 'Many prompts per file',\n        description:\n            'ptbk coder generate-boilerplates writes one prompt per file by default (--count 5*1). Use --count N*M to pack a whole backlog into fewer files: N files with M prompts each. A --- line separates the sections, every file carries one fresh emoji tag, and each section still runs as its own task.',\n        sampleCommand: GENERATE_BOILERPLATES_COMMAND,\n    },\n];\n","structuredPatch":[{"oldStart":99,"oldLines":7,"newStart":99,"newLines":7,"lines":["     {","         title: 'Pacing and retries',","         description:","-            'Wait a fixed wall-clock duration between prompts. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01B8mD3Uq4jsY1MTSv6CUjew","type":"tool_result","content":"-   Fixed the warnings printed while installing `ptbk`. Five of the ten `npm warn deprecated` lines were caused by\n    Promptbook itself and are gone, and an installation resolves 96 packages fewer than before:\n\n    -   `crypto` was declared as a dependency, although the package of that name is only a deprecated placeholder for\n        the Node.js built-in module. Node.js resolves `crypto` to its built-in module in every case, so the package was\n        downloaded and warned about without ever being used by anything.\n    -   `y-websocket-server` was declared as a dependency without being imported anywhere. The only thing which runs\n        it, `other/y-websocket-server/y-websocket.js`, starts it through `npx`, which resolves it on its own.\n    -   `glob-promise` is replaced by `glob` itself, which returns promises since its version 9 and no longer needs a\n        wrapper. `glob-promise` holds `glob` at version 8, which still depends on the deprecated `inflight`, so those\n        two warned together. All eleven call sites now go through one `findFilesByGlob` utility, which keeps the two\n        things `glob` version 8 guaranteed and the current one does not - `/` separators on Windows and a stable\n        alphabetical order - so nothing which reads the matched filenames had to change.\n    -   `express-openapi-validator` is updated to a release which uses `multer` 2 instead of the deprecated `multer` 1.\n\n    The five remaining deprecation warnings cannot be resolved from this repository. `lodash.get` and\n    `whatwg-encoding` are used by the newest `express-openapi-validator` and `jsdom` as well, `prebuild-install` is a\n    dependency of `better-sqlite3` which only its version 13 drops - and that version requires Node.js 22, while the\n    `engines` of Promptbook still allow Node.js 18 - and `crypto-js` and `@azure/openai` are deprecated by their\n    authors but really used by Promptbook.","is_error":false}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"74608ceb-c452-4e82-b385-4ad6b325ff5b","uuid":"f1084a06-d21a-4345-9761-bab0814093cf","timestamp":"2026-09-17T16:28:09.264Z","tool_use_result":{"stdout":"-   Fixed the warnings printed while installing `ptbk`. Five of the ten `npm warn deprecated` lines were caused by\n    Promptbook itself and are gone, and an installation resolves 96 packages fewer than before:\n\n    -   `crypto` was declared as a dependency, although the package of that name is only a deprecated placeholder for\n        the Node.js built-in module. Node.js resolves `crypto` to its built-in module in every case, so the package was\n        downloaded and warned about without ever being used by anything.\n    -   `y-websocket-server` was declared as a dependency without being imported anywhere. The only thing which runs\n        it, `other/y-websocket-server/y-websocket.js`, starts it through `npx`, which resolves it on its own.\n    -   `glob-promise` is replaced by `glob` itself, which returns promises since its version 9 and no longer needs a\n        wrapper. `glob-promise` holds `glob` at version 8, which still depends on the deprecated `inflight`, so those\n        two warned together. All eleven call sites now go through one `findFilesByGlob` utility, which keeps the two\n        things `glob` version 8 guaranteed and the current one does not - `/` separators on Windows and a stable\n        alphabetical order - so nothing which reads the matched filenames had to change.\n    -   `express-openapi-validator` is updated to a release which uses `multer` 2 instead of the deprecated `multer` 1.\n\n    The five remaining deprecation warnings cannot be resolved from this repository. `lodash.get` and\n    `whatwg-encoding` are used by the newest `express-openapi-validator` and `jsdom` as well, `prebuild-install` is a\n    dependency of `better-sqlite3` which only its version 13 drops - and that version requires Node.js 22, while the\n    `engines` of Promptbook still allow Node.js 18 - and `crypto-js` and `@azure/openai` are deprecated by their\n    authors but really used by Promptbook.","stderr":"","interrupted":false,"isImage":false,"noOutputExpected":false}}

Five of the ten `npm warn deprecated` lines were caused by\n    Promptbook itself and are gone, and an installation resolves 96 packages fewer than before:","new_string":"-   Made the subscription usage shown by `ptbk coder run` live. The **Usage** rows of the terminal dashboard used to be\n    read once before the queue started and then once more after each finished prompt, so for the whole round — which can\n    easily be hours — they described a moment that had already passed. They are now re-read every 5 seconds by one shared\n    refresher which the run starts once and stops when it ends, so the remaining percentages and the reset countdowns\n    always describe the present moment instead of the state the harness was in when the current prompt started. Two\n    reads never overlap: a tick which arrives while the previous read is still in flight is skipped, so a slow or\n    hanging harness cannot pile requests up, and a harness without subscription limits or a run without the dashboard\n    starts no timer at all. OpenAI Codex already answers every single read with a fresh account snapshot, while Claude\n    Code reports its limits as events of the stream it is writing — so the Claude Code runner now reads its limits from\n    the live output as well, instead of only from the finished one, which is what gives the 5-second refresh something\n    new to show in the middle of a prompt. To make that possible, every script runner can now observe completed output\n    lines while the script is still running, and the buffering which turns arbitrarily chopped chunks into whole lines\n    is shared by both of them. The `ptbk coder` landing page documents the new refresh.\n\n-   Fixed the warnings printed while installing `ptbk`. Five of the ten `npm warn deprecated` lines were caused by\n    Promptbook itself and are gone, and an installation resolves 96 packages fewer than before:","newString":"-   Made the subscription usage shown by `ptbk coder run` live. The **Usage** rows of the terminal dashboard used to be\n    read once before the queue started and then once more after each finished prompt, so for the whole round — which can\n    easily be hours — they described a moment that had already passed. They are now re-read every 5 seconds by one shared\n    refresher which the run starts once and stops when it ends, so the remaining percentages and the reset countdowns\n    always describe the present moment instead of the state the harness was in when the current prompt started. Two\n    reads never overlap: a tick which arrives while the previous read is still in flight is skipped, so a slow or\n    hanging harness cannot pile requests up, and a harness without subscription limits or a run without the dashboard\n    starts no timer at all. OpenAI Codex already answers every single read with a fresh account snapshot, while Claude\n    Code reports its limits as events of the stream it is writing — so the Claude Code runner now reads its limits from\n    the live output as well, instead of only from the finished one, which is what gives the 5-second refresh something\n    new to show in the middle of a prompt. To make that possible, every script runner can now observe completed output\n    lines while the script is still running, and the buffering which turns arbitrarily chopped chunks into whole lines\n    is shared by both of them. The `ptbk coder` landing page documents the new refresh.\n\n-   Fixed the warnings printed while installing `ptbk`. Five of the ten `npm warn deprecated` lines were caused by\n    Promptbook itself and are gone, and an installation resolves 96 packages fewer than before:","originalFile":"-   Fixed the warnings printed while installing `ptbk`. Five of the ten `npm warn deprecated` lines were caused by\n    Promptbook itself and are gone, and an installation resolves 96 packages fewer than before:\n\n    -   `crypto` was declared as a dependency, although the package of that name is only a deprecated placeholder for\n        the Node.js built-in module. Node.js resolves `crypto` to its built-in module in every case, so the package was\n        downloaded and warned about without ever being used by anything.\n    -   `y-websocket-server` was declared as a dependency without being imported anywhere. The only thing which runs\n        it, `other/y-websocket-server/y-websocket.js`, starts it through `npx`, which resolves it on its own.\n    -   `glob-promise` is replaced by `glob` itself, which returns promises since its version 9 and no longer needs a\n        wrapper. `glob-promise` holds `glob` at version 8, which still depends on the deprecated `inflight`, so those\n        two warned together. All eleven call sites now go through one `findFilesByGlob` utility, which keeps the two\n        things `glob` version 8 guaranteed and the current one does not - `/` separators on Windows and a stable\n        alphabetical order - so nothing which reads the matched filenames had to change.\n    -   `express-openapi-validator` is updated to a release which uses `multer` 2 instead of the deprecated `multer` 1.\n\n    The five remaining deprecation warnings cannot be resolved from this repository. `lodash.get` and\n    `whatwg-encoding` are used by the newest `express-openapi-validator` and `jsdom` as well, `prebuild-install` is a\n    dependency of `better-sqlite3` which only its version 13 drops - and that version requires Node.js 22, while the\n    `engines` of Promptbook still allow Node.js 18 - and `crypto-js` and `@azure/openai` are deprecated by their\n    authors but really used by Promptbook.\n\n-   Reduced what `npm audit` reports after installing `ptbk` from 48 vulnerable packages to 15, and from 3 critical\n    advisories to none. Every version pinned by Promptbook which an advisory named is raised to a release without that\n    advisory: `next` (which also carried the only critical advisories and brings its bundled `sharp` with it),\n    `express` (with `body-parser`, `qs` and `path-to-regexp`), `socket.io-client` (with `engine.io-client` and `ws`),\n    `mailparser` (with `linkify-it` and its own `nodemailer`), `@aws-sdk/client-s3` (with `fast-xml-parser`),\n    `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`, `nodemailer`, `dompurify`, `jspdf` and `postcss`. `nodemailer` is the only one which\n    crosses a major version, from 7 to 9, and Promptbook calls only its `createTransport` and `sendMail`, which those\n    versions do not change - it is now also the same installation which `mailparser` uses. `@aws-sdk/client-s3` is the\n    only one which raises its own Node.js requirement, from 18 to 20, which does not move the Node.js version an\n    installation really needs, because `better-sqlite3`, `@supabase/supabase-js` and `playwright` have all been asking\n    for Node.js 20 for longer.\n\n    What is still reported either has no fixed release at all - `showdown`, and `xlsx` inside `markitdown-ts` - or can\n    only be fixed by an upgrade which would break something else: the fixed majors of `@ai-sdk/openai`,\n    `@ai-sdk/google`, `@ai-sdk/deepseek` (together with `undici`) and `@vercel/blob` require Node.js 22, `localtunnel`\n    has no release which stops using a vulnerable `axios`, and a moderate advisory on `next` with a high one on the\n    `postcss` bundled inside it, plus `monaco-editor` with the `dompurify` bundled inside it, are only fixed by\n    upgrades of Next.js and the Monaco editor which deserve their own change.\n\n-   `ptbk coder` now resolves `FROM`, `IMPORT`, and `TEAM` references across local agent books before compiling coding\n    instructions. Names in `@Name` and `{Name}` match first-line book titles discovered recursively beneath the selected\n    agent's folder. `./` and `../` paths resolve from the declaring book, other paths from the working directory, and\n    HTTP(S) book URLs work too, including nested inheritance and imports. The coder and Agent Server share the same\n    inheritance implementation. Agents inherit from local Adam by default; a missing Adam is copied from the bundled\n    server book into `.core/adam.book`. `FROM @null`, `FROM {null}`, `FROM @void`, and `FROM {void}` disable inheritance.\n    `ptbk coder init` also creates `agents/.core/adam.book` without overwriting an existing book. Added a reference-resolution\n    test preset in VS Code and documented the reference rules on the coder landing page. Normal committing runs\n    commit a newly created Adam book before checking for a clean working tree; `--no-commit` leaves it uncommitted.\n\n-   Fixed the React 19 peer dependency warnings during `npm install` by replacing `swagger-ui-react` with the\n    standalone `swagger-ui-dist` bundle, shared with the Express API docs. The Swagger page still loads on demand\n    and keeps its API-key panel, saved authorization and display settings.\n    Test builds now skip Sentry source-map uploads to avoid temporary upload bundles and Windows cleanup failures.\n    CLI help tests use the same command registration as the executable without starting a new process for every\n    subcommand. CLI startup and version checks still run in child processes, with a timeout that stops stuck children.\n\n-   A generated system message no longer repeats the same instructions. Commitments are applied one by one, so a\n    commitment used several times in one book emitted its whole section every time, including the shared guidance\n    paragraph which introduces it. Two `WRITING RULES` blocks produced two `## Writing rules` headings each preceded by\n    the same four-line explanation of what a writing rule is, two `USE PRIVACY` blocks produced the `## Privacy`\n    instructions twice, and the same held for `WRITING SAMPLE`, `SAMPLE`, `LANGUAGE`, `USE POPUP`,\n    `USE IMAGE GENERATOR`, `USE USER LOCATION` and `TEAM`. The final system message is now deduplicated once for all\n    commitments instead of being fixed in each of them separately:\n\n    -   All sections sharing one `## Title` are merged into the position of their first occurrence, so each heading\n        appears exactly once while the content of every commitment keeps its original order inside that section.\n    -   Every identical block is kept only once, so the shared guidance paragraph of a repeated commitment is stated\n        once and a repeated instruction without its own heading, such as `STYLE Formal.` written twice, is no longer\n        duplicated.\n    -   Two lists joined by a merge become one compact list, while everything which was not merged keeps its original\n        spacing, and fenced code blocks - imported files and inline `KNOWLEDGE` content among them - are never split\n        or deduplicated.\n    -   A book which uses each of its commitments once produces the same system message as before.\n\n-   `ptbk coder` now tracks the agent of a run next to its harness and model. Two runs of the same harness, model and\n    thinking level are not the same run when one of them carries an `--agent`, so the run report of every prompt now\n    names the agent which implemented it:\n\n    -   A prompt status line signs its work with the agent in front of the harness, as\n        `` [x] by Developer on OpenAI Codex `gpt-5.6-luna` thinking `max` (ChatGPT account) - Implementation ~$0.13 23 minutes ``.\n        The `[^]`, `[x]` and `[!]` status lines and the run trace of the round all report it, and a prompt continued\n        through `--git-changes continue` keeps the agent in each of its chronological `interrupted, continued by …`\n        reports.\n    -   The reported name is the display name of the Book — its `META FULLNAME`, or the plain title on its first line\n        — so `agents/coding/developer.book` signs as its Book title and not as its normalized identifier.\n    -   A run started without `--agent` reports exactly what it reported before.\n\n-   Fixed `MockedChat` typing animations blinking for messages without ids by assigning stable playback-only ids before rendering each simulated transcript.\n\n-   Fixed the rich `ptbk coder run` dashboard so an animated agent avatar can no longer overwrite its own UI in an\n    exact-width terminal pane:\n\n    -   The shared frame layout now leaves one physical terminal column unused, preventing boxed rows from\n        auto-wrapping and keeping incremental cursor-based redraws aligned with their logical frame rows.\n    -   Added a focused VS Code terminal preset and regression coverage for the terminal-width invariant.\n\n-   Added agent-specific prompt routing to `ptbk coder`:\n\n    -   A ready `[ ]` prompt can now target the Book passed in `--agent` with a backtick-delimited path, filename,\n        filename without `.book`, or the Book title from its first line. For example, a run using\n        `--agent agents/coding/developer.book` accepts `agents/coding/developer.book`, `developer.book`,\n        `developer`, and `Promptbook Developer` routing tokens.\n    -   Agent references work alongside the existing model and harness routing tokens, and `ptbk coder list --agent\n        <path.book>` previews the same agent-specific queue without starting a harness.\n    -   Added an Unslopper agent preset next to the developer preset in the local VS Code terminal scripts and\n        documented agent-specific routing on the `ptbk coder` landing page.\n\n-   The help of `ptbk` does not advertise the deprecated commands anymore. `run`, `login`, `make`, `prettify`, `test`,\n    `list-models`, `list-scrapers`, `start-agents-server` and `start-pipelines-server` are all leftovers of the old\n    pipeline system, yet nine of the fifteen commands which `ptbk --help` listed were exactly those, each one with its\n    own `Deprecated:` paragraph, so the listing which is supposed to introduce the CLI was mostly made of commands\n    nobody should start using. `ptbk --help`, and the same listing which plain `ptbk` prints when it asks for a\n    subcommand, now offers only the commands which are meant to be used - `coder`, `agent`, `agent-folder`,\n    `agents-server`, `about` and `hello`. Nothing was removed: every deprecated command still runs, still warns that it\n    is deprecated when it is used, still explains the deprecation in its own help - `ptbk run --help` - and is still\n    reachable through `ptbk help run`. Only the \"did you mean\" hint for a mistyped command stops pointing at them.\n    Being left out of the help is now simply a part of what deprecating a command means, written once in\n    `$deprecateCliCommand`, so any command deprecated later disappears from the help on its own.\n\n-   `ptbk` without a subcommand no longer falls back to the deprecated `ptbk run`. Until now `run` was registered as\n    the default command of the CLI, so everything which did not name a command - `ptbk ./write-cv.book`, a mistyped\n    `ptbk codr` or a stray option - was quietly handed over to the pipeline runner of the old system, which was the\n    last thing a deprecated command should be doing. Plain `ptbk` now asks to specify a subcommand and prints the\n    top-level help, exactly like `ptbk coder`, `ptbk agent`, `ptbk agent-folder` and `ptbk agents-server` already did\n    when they were called without one of their own subcommands, and that one shared behavior is now written once\n    instead of five times. Anything which is not a command is refused with `unknown command` and a \"did you mean\"\n    hint instead of being executed as a pipeline, so a script which still passes a book path to `ptbk` fails loudly\n    rather than appearing to succeed. `ptbk run` itself is untouched and keeps working for everyone who asks for it\n    explicitly. The command list in the help now starts with `coder`, followed by `agent`, `agent-folder` and\n    `agents-server`, and the deprecated commands of the old pipeline system are listed after them.\n\n-   `ptbk coder` now saves the run trace of every prompt round, so a finished run can still be analyzed afterwards.\n    Until now the only durable record of a round was the one status line written into the prompt file: the live\n    runtime log holding everything the harness and the verification command had written was a temporary artifact,\n    deleted as soon as a successful round was over unless `--preserve-logs` was passed, and lost together with the\n    reasoning, the tool calls and the diffs of the run. Each round now writes `prompts/traces/<prompt-file-name>.md`\n    - a trace named exactly like the prompt file it belongs to, with the same `-2` section suffix the temporary\n    scripts of a multi-section prompt file already use. The trace pairs the metadata of the round - which prompt and\n    section it implemented, whether it succeeded or failed, the harness, model, thinking level and login method which\n    ran it, how many coding attempts it took, what each step cost and how long each one ran, the verification\n    command, the start, end and duration, and the error which ended a failed round - with the untouched runtime log\n    of the harness. Because the trace is written before the round is committed, it lands in the very same commit as\n    the prompt it describes, and a task whose isolated worktree cannot be merged back carries its trace into the\n    failure commit instead. A failed round is traced too, next to the `.error.log` it already wrote. Re-running the\n    same prompt overwrites its trace and leaves the earlier ones in the git history.\n\n-   `ptbk coder run` and `ptbk coder server` no longer walk into a full disk. A coding round writes prompt and log\n    artifacts, lets the harness rewrite the project, may install npm packages, may create a git worktree for\n    `--isolate` and usually runs a build, so a run started without enough space used to die somewhere in the middle,\n    after the coding agent had already rewritten a part of the project. The free disk space is now measured before\n    anything is installed or written: with less than 2 GB left the command refuses to start and says how much space\n    is left, how much is needed and how to get it back, instead of failing later with a raw filesystem error. The\n    same measurement is repeated while the run is in progress - at the checkpoints where `ptbk coder` can stop\n    anyway, so it is checked before every round, every verification and every commit - and once less than 1 GB is\n    left the run reports the same warning and pauses there, waiting for the disk space to be freed and for `P` to\n    resume it. The limit to keep running is lower than the limit to start, because interrupting a round which is\n    already in progress costs more than not starting one. A run started with `--no-questions` never pauses, because\n    there is nobody who could free the disk space and resume it - it reports the warning and keeps going. A platform\n    which cannot report its free disk space never stops a run.\n\n-   Added `--no-questions` to every `ptbk coder` command which can stop and wait for an answer it does not strictly\n    need. `init`, `add`, `run`, `ping` and `server` still do all their work, but no longer ask anything: installing\n    a missing coding harness, updating an outdated one, updating an outdated Promptbook CLI and adding the missing\n    harness ignore rules to `.gitignore` are all skipped and reported together with the command which does them\n    manually, and `ptbk coder add` refuses a missing description instead of asking for it. Because an outdated\n    harness or CLI can only be updated after a confirmation, `--no-questions` also skips the npm latest-version\n    lookup which would only lead to a question, which is what the never released `--no-harness-update` used to do -\n    that flag is replaced by `--no-questions` and is gone. The one combination which can not work,\n    `--no-auto --no-questions`, is refused right away instead of waiting forever for a confirmation nobody may be\n    asked for. `ptbk coder verify` does not take the flag, because walking through finished prompts and asking about\n    each of them is the only thing it does.\n\n-   `ptbk coder` no longer answers a harness which is not logged in with a wall of raw CLI output. A harness whose\n    login is missing or whose session has expired now fails with a short branded `AuthenticationError` which names\n    the harness, quotes the one sentence the harness itself reported - such as `Failed to authenticate: OAuth session\n    expired and could not be refreshed` - and says exactly how to sign in again, for example by running `claude` and\n    then the `/login` command inside it. How each harness is signed in is described once, next to how it is installed\n    and detected, and the failure is recognized once for every harness and for every command\n    which runs prompts, so `coder run`, `coder server` and `coder ping` all report it the same way. The terminal and\n    the `.error.log` file written next to the prompt both show those instructions on their own now, instead of\n    following them with a stack trace of a failure nobody can debug. Because no retry of a harness which is not\n    logged in can ever succeed, such a prompt is also no longer retried three times with the `--wait-after-error`\n    delay in between - the instructions are shown right away.\n\n-   Fixed the wall of `npm warn ERESOLVE overriding peer dependency` warnings printed when installing `ptbk`:\n\n    -   The Vercel AI SDK providers `@ai-sdk/openai`, `@ai-sdk/google` and `@ai-sdk/deepseek` were still on the\n        generation which accepts only Zod 3, while the rest of the ecosystem - the Agents Server, `@openai/agents`,\n        `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` - needs Zod 4. No single Zod could satisfy both sides, so npm reported a conflict\n        for every one of those packages. They are upgraded to the newest generation which accepts both Zod 3 and\n        Zod 4 and still runs on Node.js 18, so the supported Node.js versions of Promptbook do not change, and\n        `createExecutionToolsFromVercelProvider` is migrated to the model interface of that generation. Settings\n        given as `additionalChatSettings` are now passed to the model call instead of to the model constructor,\n        which is where the Vercel AI SDK expects them, and the `userId` option is no longer sent as the `user`\n        setting, because it has become specific to each provider.\n    -   Generated packages no longer publish dependencies which only look like imports. Package generation infers\n        dependencies by reading the generated bundle, and it used to count module specifiers written inside the\n        source-code templates of the transpilers, so `@promptbook/core` published `zod`, `dotenv` and\n        `@anthropic-ai/sdk` as runtime dependencies although it never imports any of them. The pinned `zod` in\n        particular forced one exact Zod version onto every project which installs Promptbook.\n    -   Generated packages no longer carry the `overrides` field of the repository. npm honors overrides only in the\n        root project of an installation, so publishing them only left a dangling reference to a dependency which the\n        published package does not declare.\n\n-   The hero headline of the **ptbk coder** landing page now rotates through seven claims instead of saying one\n    thing forever. Every claim is written once in a single configuration the rotating headline, the page tagline\n    and the sharing image all read, and the claims crossfade with a slight vertical slide - the claim which leaves\n    rises out of the headline while the next one rises into it. All claims share one grid cell, so the headline\n    keeps the height of the tallest of them and nothing around it moves while they rotate. The same reserved\n    height finally balances the hero: together with a terminal text size tuned one step down, the copy column now\n    reaches almost as high as the live terminal next to it, instead of floating in the middle of a section the\n    terminal alone defines. Visitors whose system prefers reduced motion keep the first claim without rotation.\n\n-   Fixed `ptbk coder init` overwriting configuration the project already owns. Existing `package.json` scripts and\n    `.vscode/settings.json` settings are now kept verbatim and only genuinely missing ones are added. Files a default\n    script points at, like `agents/developer.book`, `AGENTS.md` and `prompts/templates/common.md`, are created only\n    together with the script which references them, so a project with its own `coder:run` no longer receives an unused\n    default agent. `ptbk coder init` also initializes the `test-for-ptbk-coder` npm script which the default\n    `coder:run` uses as its verification command.\n\n-   Rebalanced the hero of the **ptbk coder** landing page, whose live terminal used to be much taller than the copy\n    next to it and left the headline, the install command and the buttons floating in the middle of a section the\n    terminal alone defined:\n\n    -   The terminal window is now never wider than the character grid it draws, so a layout with more width than the\n        widest supported terminal - a tablet, a phone in landscape - gets a centered window instead of a window with an\n        empty half, and it fills the height of the copy column whenever the copy is the taller one.\n    -   A terminal row is now as tight as a real terminal emulator draws it, which both shortens the sample session by\n        about one tenth and keeps the frames of the dashboard boxes connected.\n    -   The box drawing characters, the shade of the progress bar and the status marks are missing from the latin\n        subset of the terminal font, so they were drawn from the fallback which `next/font` derives from a\n        **proportional** font - about one and a half character cells wide and shorter than one row, which broke every\n        box border of the dashboard into detached segments. The terminal font now falls back to the monospace fonts of\n        the system, so those characters are drawn one cell wide and one row tall and the boxes are drawn as continuous\n        frames.\n    -   The hero copy is now read at hero size: the headline and the subheadline grow with the viewport, but only as\n        far as their own column can carry them, so the headline keeps its two lines from the narrowest phone to the\n        widest desktop.\n\n-   Fixed `ptbk coder init` so it no longer creates an `AGENT_CODING.md` quick-reference file.\n-   Redesigned the three core benefit illustrations on the **ptbk coder** landing page with detailed terminal,\n    portable-agent, and synchronized-commit scenes, plus proportional graphics and a more readable tablet layout.\n\n-   Fixed `ptbk coder init` to preserve a non-empty `prompts/` directory instead of adding placeholder boilerplate\n    prompts while it initializes the remaining coder files.\n\n-   Added `ptbk coder list`, a read-only queue preview that lists ready, fully authored prompts in descending priority\n    groups without starting a harness. Its optional `--harness`, `--model`, `--priority`, `--min-priority`, and\n    `--max-priority` filters let you preview exactly the queue a selected runner would receive.\n\n-   Added a live GitHub star counter and **Star on GitHub** call to action to the **ptbk coder** landing page.\n\n-   Added support for plain markdown prompts without a status checkbox in **ptbk coder**. `ptbk coder run` and\n    `ptbk coder server` now treat them as ready prompts at priority `0`, then insert the normal live `[^]` status line\n    before their content as processing begins and finish them through the usual `[x]` or `[!]` flow.\n\n-   Added queue opt-out markers to **ptbk coder**. `[.]` now behaves like `[-]`, keeping that prompt out of the queue,\n    and `<!--ptbk-coder-ignore-->` anywhere in a Markdown prompt file excludes the entire file from `run`, `list`, and\n    `server`.\n\n-   Added project-local harness ignore rules to **ptbk coder**. `ptbk coder init` now adds the rules for every supported\n    harness, including `.qwen`; `ptbk coder run`, `ptbk coder server`, and `ptbk coder ping` detect a missing selected\n    harness rule and use the same interactive `[y/N]` confirmation as harness installation updates before adding it.\n\n-   Fixed globally installing `ptbk` on Node.js 26, including macOS arm64. `ptbk coder` can now be installed without\n    `better-sqlite3` 11 falling back to a native build against removed V8 APIs; the generated CLI now receives\n    `better-sqlite3` 12.11.1, which supplies the matching Node 26 binary.\n\n-   Fixed the Agents Server production build failing when its Edge middleware reached standalone SQLite code.\n    SQLite registry loading now lives in a Node.js-only module, and custom-domain routing reads its needed federation\n    settings through the middleware's supplied Supabase client. Edge middleware can therefore route configured domains\n    without compiling `better-sqlite3` into its bundle.\n\n-   Fixed `ptbk coder --harness openai-codex --model default` failing for everyone signed in to OpenAI Codex with a\n    ChatGPT account. `default` silently stood for `gpt-5.2-codex`, which such an account rejects with\n    _\"The 'gpt-5.2-codex' model is not supported when using Codex with a ChatGPT account\"_ — so both\n    `ptbk coder ping` and `ptbk coder run` died before doing any work.\n\n    -   `--model default` now overrides **no model at all** for OpenAI Codex: Codex is started without `--model` and\n        keeps the model from its own configuration _(`~/.codex/config.toml`)_, exactly like `--model default` already\n        worked for GitHub Copilot. Whatever a ChatGPT-account login is allowed to use therefore works.\n    -   Naming a model explicitly, for example `--model gpt-5.2-codex`, is unchanged, and `--model` is still required\n        for OpenAI Codex.\n    -   For `gemini` and `qwen-code`, `default` keeps standing for their concrete default model, because those CLIs\n        have no configured default to fall back to.\n    -   When Codex picks the model itself, the reported price is estimated from the fallback pricing, because only\n        Codex knows which model it really used.\n\n-   Fixed **ptbk coder** updating a coding harness with `npm install -g` even when npm does not own that harness. A\n    Codex installed by the official standalone installer was reported as outdated and \"updated\" into a _second_ Codex\n    inside the active Node prefix, while the Codex which actually runs stayed on its old version — and which of the two\n    was used from then on depended on the active Node version.\n\n    -   Before offering an update, `ptbk coder` now resolves which file the harness command really executes _(following\n        symbolic links, using the very same `PATH` which runs the harness)_ and recognizes whether it belongs to a\n        global npm installation, a standalone installation, or Homebrew.\n    -   A **standalone installation is updated with its own updater** — `codex update` for OpenAI Codex — and a\n        **Homebrew installation is never touched**, only `brew upgrade …` is printed. When the harness command cannot\n        be traced to any of these, `ptbk coder` says so and leaves it alone instead of guessing, because\n        `npm install -g` would install a second copy next to it.\n    -   The outdated-harness warning now also prints the resolved command path and how it was installed, and the\n        confirmation question names the exact command which is about to run, so an update can no longer be approved\n        without knowing what it does.\n    -   Installing a harness which is missing altogether is unchanged: it is still installed globally through npm.\n\n-   Added the singular `WRITING RULE` keyword as an equivalent variant of `WRITING RULES`, exactly like `RULE` and\n    `RULES` are interchangeable. Both spellings are parsed, applied, documented, and syntax-highlighted identically, so\n    a single writing constraint no longer has to be written in plural.\n\n-   Fixed the Agents Server starting one more pm2 process of the same agent project on every single start, which\n    eventually took the whole server down.\n\n    -   Every project runtime is registered under a stable pm2 process name, and a project was expected to be replaced\n        rather than duplicated because it is deleted right before it is started again. That delete was **skipped\n        whenever pm2 could not be asked for its process list**, and `pm2 start` appends a second process instead of\n        refusing a name it already knows, so each start added one more copy of the same project.\n    -   The process list could not be read because `pm2 jlist` embeds a full environment snapshot into every listed\n        process — roughly 70 kB each — while its output was capped at one megabyte. A dozen projects were enough to\n        exceed that cap, after which **every** pm2 query failed with `ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER` and reported\n        every process as unknown. Each new duplicate made the output larger, so the failure never recovered on its own.\n    -   Every duplicate got its own port but the project's dev command kept binding the port it had chosen itself, so\n        all but one copy crash-looped on `EADDRINUSE`, and pm2 restarted them hundreds of times per hour until the VPS\n        ran out of threads (`pthread_create: Resource temporarily unavailable`) and the Agents Server itself was\n        killed.\n    -   Deleting a project process no longer depends on reading the process list: it is always attempted, only pm2\n        itself reporting an unknown name counts as \"already gone\", and any other failure is reported instead of\n        swallowed — so a project is now left alone rather than duplicated when pm2 misbehaves. Because `pm2 delete`\n        removes every process sharing one name, a server which already accumulated duplicates converges back to a\n        single process per project.\n\n-   Added the **Qwen Code** harness, so `ptbk coder` now drives seven coding agents instead of six.\n\n    -   `ptbk coder run --harness qwen-code --model qwen3.8-max` runs the whole prompt queue through the Qwen Code CLI,\n        and every other harness-aware command — `ptbk coder ping`, `ptbk coder server`, `ptbk agent exec`, `CliAgent`\n        and the `PTBK_HARNESS` environment variable — accepts `qwen-code` the same way.\n    -   Like `openai-codex` and `gemini`, Qwen Code **requires an explicit `--model`**; `--model default` resolves to\n        `qwen3.8-max`. Its global `@qwen-code/qwen-code` installation is checked and updated before the first prompt,\n        just like the other harnesses. Qwen Code exposes no reasoning-effort flag, so `--thinking-level` does not\n        apply to it.\n    -   Price estimation of harnesses which do not report their own token counts is now shared between Qwen Code and\n        Gemini instead of being written twice.\n\n-   Fixed generated `ptbk` prompt emoji tags so `coder add`, `coder generate-boilerplates`, refactor prompt generation, and `coder find-fresh-emoji-tags` share one Unicode-valid single-pictogram catalogue instead of a duplicated legacy list containing non-emoji symbols. The emoji-tag scan cache now records the candidate catalogue fingerprint and rescans when it changes, so an already assigned tag such as `[✨🛼]` is not mistaken for a fresh tag after an update.\n\n-   Added remaining subscription-limit visibility to the rich **ptbk coder** terminal dashboard.\n\n    -   The `Session` box now lists every rolling limit a selected harness reports, including its remaining percentage\n        and reset time. It does not assume a fixed pair of windows, so a 5-hour, weekly, model-specific, or future\n        additional limit all render as separate aligned rows.\n    -   OpenAI Codex reads its current account snapshot through the Codex app-server protocol, while Claude Code\n        reuses its normal `stream-json` rate-limit events instead of spending a separate quota-only prompt. Other\n        harnesses keep their existing behavior until they implement the same optional runner capability.\n    -   Updated the **ptbk coder** landing-page terminal demo and pacing copy to show the new 5-hour and 7-day\n        subscription rows.\n\n-   Let you decide what **ptbk coder** does with a dirty working tree. The clean-working-tree guard used to be a yes/no\n    question — either the coder refused to start, or `--ignore-git-changes` waved the changes through. The far more\n    common case had no answer at all: a run that was killed or crashed mid-task, leaving half-finished work in the tree\n    and one prompt stuck in the in-progress `[^]` status. The only way forward was to throw that work away.\n\n    -   **The new `--git-changes <fail|ignore|continue>` replaces `--ignore-git-changes`**, which is gone; use\n        `--git-changes ignore` instead. `fail` stays the default and now says in its error which of the other two modes\n        to reach for.\n    -   **`--git-changes continue` resumes the interrupted prompt** with its uncommitted changes still in place. It\n        expects **exactly one** prompt in the `[^]` status and refuses to guess otherwise: finding none or finding\n        several fails with a message naming the prompts it found, because the changes in the tree cannot be attributed\n        to a single task. Only that one round runs on the dirty tree — once it is committed, every later round expects a\n        clean working tree again. It cannot be combined with `--isolate`, whose fresh worktree is checked out from the\n        last commit and would leave exactly those changes behind, or `--test-before yes-and-fix`, which has no\n        unmodified project state to verify and repair.\n    -   **A prompt one harness started and another one finished says so in chronological order.** A resumed status\n        now reads `` [^] by OpenAI Codex `gpt-5.6-luna` thinking `max`, interrupted, continued by Claude Code `claude-opus-5` thinking `high` - Implementation in progress ``,\n        and the `[x]` and `[!]` lines keep that report. Each further `--git-changes continue` invocation extends the\n        same report with another `interrupted, continued by …` segment, so no earlier harness is dropped; resuming the\n        same harness keeps its existing authentication label instead of naming it twice. The live status still reports\n        its active phase, but the final continuation report omits its partial step usage and duration rather than\n        presenting them as the whole task. All three statuses go through one\n        [`formatPromptRunnerAttribution`](../scripts/run-codex-prompts/prompts/promptRunnerAttribution.ts), which also\n        understands the reverse-ordered `started by` status lines written by the preceding version.\n    -   `ptbk coder server` and `ptbk agent-folder run` share the same flag. An agent folder answers queued messages\n        instead of running a prompt queue, so `continue` keeps the changes there exactly like `ignore` does.\n\n-   Made the terminal controls of **ptbk coder** answer every key press. Pressing `P`, `S` or `X` used to be a leap of\n    faith: `S Skip current waiting` in particular changed nothing on screen, so there was no way to tell whether the key\n    had arrived, whether the wait was being skipped, or whether the terminal had simply stopped repainting.\n\n    -   **Every press is now answered inside the `Controls` box**, on the frame that follows it, for example\n        `» S Skipping the current waiting, continuing right now`. A press which changes nothing is answered too\n        (`» S Nothing to skip, the coder is not waiting right now`), because \"nothing happened\" and \"the key was lost\"\n        must not look the same. The answer fades after a few seconds and repeated identical answers are counted\n        (`(×2)`), so even pressing the same control twice redraws the frame.\n    -   **`S` now really skips the wait it is offered for.** The control is shown during every `waiting` phase, but two\n        of those waits were never registered as skippable and quietly ignored the key: the Claude Code session-limit\n        wait before a `--resume` resurrection, which can hold a run for hours, and the `ptbk coder server` keep-alive\n        poll. Both go through\n        [`waitForSkippableWorldTimeDeadline`](../scripts/run-codex-prompts/common/waitForSkippableWorldTimeDeadline.ts)\n        now, the single way the coder waits for a deadline the user may cut short, which\n        [`sleepWithCountdown`](../scripts/run-codex-prompts/common/sleepWithCountdown.ts) already used for the pacing\n        and error waits.\n    -   **The keys are handled in exactly one place.** The rich terminal UI and the plain `--no-ui` console listener\n        each had their own copy of the `P`/`S`/`X` dispatch, and only the plain one said anything back.\n        [`applyCoderRunControlKey`](../scripts/run-codex-prompts/common/applyCoderRunControlKey.ts) performs the action\n        and describes it, and both front ends render that one description through\n        [`formatCoderRunControlFeedback`](../scripts/run-codex-prompts/common/formatCoderRunControlFeedback.ts). The\n        `ptbk agent-folder run` dashboard, which shares the same renderer, answers its controls the same way.\n\n-   Took the ASCII `PTBK.IO` wordmark out of the **ptbk coder** terminal dashboard. The area above the `Session` box now\n    stays empty until the `--agent` avatar has been rendered, instead of being filled with a block-character logo that\n    was only ever a placeholder. It flashed at every start-up, and it stayed on screen for the whole run whenever no\n    agent was selected or its avatar could not be rasterized.\n\n    -   The header is still decided in one place,\n        [`buildFrameHeaderVisual`](../scripts/run-codex-prompts/ui/buildCoderRunUiFrame.ts): it draws the agent avatar\n        as soon as [`buildCoderRunAgentVisual`](../scripts/run-codex-prompts/ui/buildCoderRunAgentVisual.ts) hands one\n        over, and draws nothing before that.\n    -   `buildCoderRunOctopusVisual.ts`, which existed only to paint that wordmark, is gone.\n\n-   Simplified the comparison table on the **ptbk coder** landing page. Fifteen rows became nine, and the three agent\n    columns stopped repeating themselves: where Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and opencode make the same claim, the table\n    draws one cell across all three instead of printing the same sentence side by side three times. Exactly one row\n    still splits them, the one about moving your agent to another vendor, and that is the row worth stopping at.\n\n    -   **The rows that carried no signal are gone.** \"Human in the loop\" was a check mark in all four columns, which\n        tells a visitor nothing, and the features section explains it anyway. Thin slices of one idea were merged:\n        tests before the first task and tests after every task are one row now, and the three separate git rows\n        (commit identity, pull and push, worktree per task) are one.\n    -   **The support levels mean something again.** The matrix already ruled that anything you can script yourself is\n        `do-it-yourself` and never `not-available`, yet pacing and pre-flight tests were marked `not-available`.\n        `not-available` now means the tool has no such concept, such as a queue or a backlog, while `do-it-yourself`\n        means it hands you the pieces, such as a hook or a session to ask in.\n    -   Every claim about a compared harness is written once in the data instead of three times, so the two products\n        that genuinely differ cannot drift apart by a typo. Notes of `ptbk coder` cells are now the flag or command\n        itself, which is what makes them render in monospace, and a long one like `--wait-between-prompts` breaks\n        inside the word instead of spilling into the neighbouring column.\n\n-   Rewrote the copy of the **ptbk coder** landing page so it reads like a developer wrote it.
